summary: Our NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 project, “Be an Earth system trend detective”, investigates how Saharan dust travels across the Atlantic Ocean to the Amazon rainforest, and whether it is linked to changes in vegetation. Using monthly NASA data from 2013 to 2025, we build time series for dust density and dust emission and deposition (MERRA-2), wind speed at 10 m and 850 hPa over the Sahara and Atlantic, and Amazon vegetation health (MODIS NDVI and EVI). A Python tool lets users choose any two variables, then plots them and fits a linear regression, reporting the p value and R². We look for trends, seasonal cycles and statistical relationships between wind, dust and vegetation. Our results show association, not proof of cause, because regional monthly averages cannot track individual dust plumes.
details:
What it does and how it works

The project studies the Sahara, Atlantic and Amazon pathway. We built monthly time series for 2013-2025 from NASA data: dust density and dust emission and deposition (MERRA-2), wind speed at 10 m and 850 hPa, and amazon vegetation (MODIS NDVI and EVI). A Python tool lets the user pick any variable to plot with respect with time. It matches them month by month, plots them, fits a linear regression, and saves a PNG showing the line and p value. Three fixed regions are used throughout so that results are comparable.

Results from our dust data show that the Sahara emits roughly 420-520 Tg of dust per year. About 4% of that is deposited in the Amazon on average

Benefits and intended impact

The tool makes satellite and reanalysis data easy to explore without coding, so students and researchers can test their own questions about dust, wind and vegetation. We want to show how dust moving between continents may relate to Amazon ecosystems, and to help people see Earth systems as linked across oceans.

Tools and technology

  • Python 3.14 in VS Code, on a Windows laptop (Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM).
  • NASA Earthdata, accessed with the earthaccess and pydap libraries.
  • xarray, numpy and pandas for processing the data, and scipy for regression and p values.
  • matplotlib for graphs.
  • pyhdf for reading MODIS vegetation files.
  • Data products: MERRA-2 (aerosol, wind) and MODIS (NDVI, EVI).

Creativity

Instead of studying dust, wind or vegetation separately, we connect all three along one real transport route. The tool lets users choose their own axes, so it supports many questions, not just ours.

Factors we considered

  • Consistent regions and time period: the same boundaries and the same 156 months are used for every variable.
  • Different measures: dust optical thickness and dust mass density are kept separate, and we use true wind speed rather than the speed of averaged wind.
  • Data size: we use regional subse ts, because downloading global files would be too slow.
  • Limits of the method: regional monthly averages show association, not cause, and cannot track individual dust plumes.
